options.content: The system of rights under which land is held and used
options.rationale: Correct: tenure covers who controls land, for how long and what the holder may do with it.

options.content: The physical features of the land, such as slope and altitude
options.rationale: This is topography.

options.content: The amount of crop harvested from each hectare of land
options.rationale: This is yield.

options.content: The process of dividing a farm into fields and paddocks
options.rationale: This is farm planning (farm layout).

explanation: Land tenure is the set of rules and rights by which land is held: freehold, leasehold, communal and resettlement tenure are the systems in Zimbabwe.

stem: Under which tenure system does the holder have a **title deed** and may sell the land?

options.content: Freehold
options.rationale: Correct: a freehold owner holds a title deed and may sell, mortgage or pass on the land.

options.content: Communal
options.rationale: Communal land is vested in the state; families have only the right to use it.

options.content: Leasehold
options.rationale: A lessee rents the land for a period; it belongs to someone else.

options.content: Resettlement under a permit
options.rationale: A permit gives the right to use state land; it is not ownership.

explanation: Freehold tenure is private ownership with a title deed, held permanently.

stem: Who allocates arable land to households in a communal area of Zimbabwe?

options.content: Traditional leaders together with the rural district council
options.rationale: Correct: chiefs, headmen and village heads allocate land, working with the rural district council.

options.content: A commercial bank, in return for a mortgage
options.rationale: Banks lend money; they do not allocate communal land.

options.content: The Grain Marketing Board, according to past deliveries
options.rationale: The GMB buys and stores grain; it does not allocate land.

options.content: The household that farmed the plot first, by sale
options.rationale: Communal land cannot be sold.

explanation: Communal land is vested in the state and allocated by traditional leaders (chiefs, headmen, village heads) together with the rural district council.

stem: Why do communal farmers often find it hard to get a bank loan to develop their land?

options.content: Communal land is always too dry for farming
options.rationale: Communal areas are found in all natural regions; dryness is not the reason.

options.content: Banks are not allowed to lend money to farmers
options.rationale: Banks do lend to farmers when they have security.

options.content: They have no title deed to offer as collateral
options.rationale: Correct: without a title deed there is no security the bank can hold.

options.content: Communal farmers are not allowed to grow cash crops
options.rationale: Communal farmers may grow cash crops such as cotton and tobacco.

explanation: Communal farmers have the right to use land but no title deed, so they cannot mortgage it. This limits borrowing and long-term investment.

stem: Which law of 1930 divided the land of the colony into separate areas for European and African occupation?

options.content: The Land Acquisition Act
options.rationale: The Land Acquisition Act was passed after independence, in 1992.

options.content: The Native Land Husbandry Act
options.rationale: This act of 1951 tried to control land use and stock numbers in the reserves.

options.content: The Land Apportionment Act
options.rationale: Correct: the Land Apportionment Act of 1930 divided land along racial lines.

options.content: The Fast Track Land Reform Programme
options.rationale: This programme began in 2000; it is not a colonial law.

explanation: The Land Apportionment Act (1930) set aside separate European and African areas; Africans were moved into reserves, many of them in drier, less fertile areas.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the **A1** resettlement model?

options.content: Large self-contained commercial farms held on long leases
options.rationale: This describes the A2 model.

options.content: Private farms bought with a title deed from the state
options.rationale: Resettlement land is state land held under permits or leases, not freehold.

options.content: Land set aside for national parks and safari areas
options.rationale: This is a protected area, not a resettlement model.

options.content: Small-scale plots that relieve crowded communal areas
options.rationale: Correct: A1 gives smaller plots, often villagised with shared grazing, to families with little or no land.

explanation: A1 aims to decongest communal areas and give land to the landless; plots are small-scale, either villagised or self-contained. A2 creates commercial farms.
hints: One model is about relieving congestion; the other is about commercial farming.

stem: Shared grazing land in a communal area is often overgrazed. Which feature of communal tenure best explains this?

options.content: The grazing land has a title deed held by the chief
options.rationale: Communal land has no title deed; it is vested in the state.

options.content: No single user benefits from limiting his own herd
options.rationale: Correct: each owner gains from adding animals, but the cost of overgrazing is shared by all.

options.content: The land is leased for a short period at a high rent
options.rationale: Communal land is not leased or rented.

options.content: Fences divide the grazing into private paddocks
options.rationale: Communal grazing is usually unfenced and shared.

explanation: When grazing is shared and unfenced, each owner gains from keeping more animals while the damage is spread over everyone, so herds grow beyond the carrying capacity.
hints: Who loses when one family adds more cattle to shared grazing?

stem: A settler holds a resettlement plot under a permit. Which change would most likely encourage her to invest in a borehole and an orchard?

options.content: Shorter permits renewed by the authorities each year
options.rationale: Short, uncertain tenure discourages long-term investment.

options.content: Sharing her plot with two more families
options.rationale: Smaller plots reduce the return on investment.

options.content: A rule forbidding her from growing cash crops
options.rationale: This would lower her income and her ability to invest.

options.content: Longer, more secure tenure that lenders accept
options.rationale: Correct: secure tenure lets her borrow and assures her she will benefit from long-term investments.

explanation: Farmers invest in boreholes, fences, orchards and conservation works when tenure is secure for long enough to benefit, and when it can be used to raise credit.
hints: Think about security and access to credit.

stem: Under communal tenure a family may sell its arable land to another family.
explanation: False. Communal land is vested in the state. Families have the right to use it, but they may not sell it.

stem: Before colonial rule, land in Zimbabwe was held by the community and allocated to families by the chief.
explanation: True. The chief acted as custodian on behalf of the ancestors and allocated land through headmen; land could not be sold.

stem: Match each tenure system with its description.

right.content: State land allocated by traditional leaders; grazing shared
State-acquired land allocated to settlers under permits or leases
Permanent private ownership with a title deed
Use of another owner's land for a fixed period in return for rent

explanation: The systems differ in who holds the land, for how long and whether it can be sold or used as collateral.

stem: Choose the correct word for each blank.

payload.template: The Fast Track Land Reform Programme began in {{blank:a}}. The {{blank:b}} model was designed to create indigenous commercial farmers.

explanation: Fast-track land reform started in 2000. A1 is small-scale resettlement; A2 is commercial resettlement.

stem: Name the document that proves private (freehold) ownership of a piece of land.
explanation: A title deed proves freehold ownership and can be used as collateral for a loan.

stem: In which year did Zimbabwe gain independence, after which the first resettlement programme began?
explanation: Zimbabwe became independent in 1980. In the 1980s land was bought for resettlement on a willing-buyer, willing-seller basis.

stem: Explain **two** reasons why land is regarded as a national heritage in Zimbabwe.

points.description: Land is the base of food production, jobs and the economy.
Explains that the nation's food security and livelihoods depend on it.
Land holds ancestral graves, shrines and sacred sites / is tied to identity.
Explains that it links families and communities to their history and culture, so it must be kept for future generations.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Land is the base of farming, mining and other work, so the country's food and income depend on it. It also holds ancestral graves and sacred sites, which give people their identity and link them to their history, so it must be protected for future generations.

explanation: Each reason earns a mark, and a second mark for explaining why it matters.
hints: Think of economic reasons and cultural reasons.

stem: State **four** reasons for land reform in Zimbabwe after independence.

points.description: To correct the unequal distribution of land inherited from the colonial period.
To decongest overcrowded communal areas.
To give land to the landless and poor families.
To create indigenous commercial farmers / bring under-used land into production.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: To correct the unequal land distribution of the colonial period; to relieve overcrowding in communal areas; to give land to landless families; to create indigenous commercial farmers and use under-used land.

explanation: One mark for each distinct reason.
hints: Think about fairness, congestion, the landless and production.

stem: Describe **two** benefits and **two** problems that have been recognised since the land reform programme.

points.description: Benefit: many more families gained access to land.
Benefit: congestion in some communal areas was reduced / ownership was spread more widely / new farmers entered cash crops.
Problem: many new farmers lacked capital, equipment, inputs or skills, so production on some farms fell.
Problem: permits/leases not always accepted as collateral / tenure insecurity and boundary disputes / infrastructure deteriorated / farm workers lost jobs.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: More families now have land, and crowding in some communal areas was eased. However, many new farmers lacked money, equipment and skills, so output on some farms fell, and their permits are not always accepted by banks as security, which makes borrowing difficult.

explanation: A balanced answer gives both benefits and problems, stated factually.

stem:
Table 1 describes three fictional farmers.

**Table 1**

| Farmer | Area | How the land is held | Grazing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Farmer K | Communal area | Field allocated by the village head | Shares grazing with the village |
| Farmer L | Commercial farm | Bought the farm; holds a title deed | Own fenced paddocks |
| Farmer M | Resettlement area | Plot allocated under a government permit | Shares grazing with other settlers |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which tenure system does farmer L hold the land under?

options.content: Communal
options.rationale: Communal land is allocated, not bought.

options.content: Freehold
options.rationale: Correct: L bought the farm and holds a title deed.

options.content: Resettlement
options.rationale: Resettlement land is held under a permit or lease.

options.content: Leasehold
options.rationale: L owns the land; it is not rented.

parts.explanation: A title deed shows freehold ownership.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the tenure system of farmer K.
parts.explanation: Land allocated by the village head with shared grazing is communal tenure.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why farmer L finds it easier than farmer K to get a bank loan.

points.description: L has a title deed that can be used as collateral / security.
K has only the right to use the land, which cannot be mortgaged, so the bank has no security.

parts.explanation: Security of tenure and a title deed make borrowing easier.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** problem farmers K and M may face because their grazing is shared.

points.description: Overgrazing / too many animals on the shared land.
Explains that no one controls numbers, so grass cover is lost and the soil erodes (or diseases spread between herds).

parts.explanation: Shared, unfenced grazing is easily overstocked.

explanation: Tenure decides access to credit and how land is managed.
hints: Which farmer has something a bank will accept as security?

stem: After independence the government of Zimbabwe carried out land reform, first by buying land and later through the Fast Track Land Reform Programme, which resettled people under the A1 and A2 models.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how land was held in Zimbabwe before colonial rule.

points.description: Land belonged to the community and was held by the chief as custodian.
Families were allocated land to use through headmen; it could not be sold / grazing was shared.

parts.explanation: Pre-colonial tenure was communal, under the chief.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Compare the A1 and A2 resettlement models.

points.description: Aim: A1 decongests communal areas / helps the landless; A2 creates commercial farmers.
Scale: A1 small-scale plots; A2 small- to large-scale commercial farms.
Layout: A1 villagised or self-contained with shared grazing; A2 self-contained farms.
Tenure: A1 permits; A2 leases (long leases).

parts.explanation: Each comparison point must mention both models.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Discuss the effects of the land reform programme on agriculture in Zimbabwe.

points.description: More families gained access to land / ownership spread more widely.
Congestion and pressure on some communal areas reduced.
New farmers entered crops such as tobacco and maize, many supported by contract farming.
Many new farmers lacked capital, equipment, inputs and skills, so production on some farms fell.
Tenure insecurity / permits not accepted as collateral / boundary disputes discouraged investment; some infrastructure deteriorated; farm workers lost jobs.
Balanced conclusion weighing benefits against problems (e.g. access widened, but secure tenure, credit and support decide whether farms are productive).

levels.descriptor: Accurate, well-developed explanation of several relevant points using correct agricultural terms, applied to the crop, animal or situation in the question, with a clear judgement where one is asked for.
Some relevant points explained, partly developed or only partly applied to the situation; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.

parts.explanation: A discussion needs both benefits and problems, stated factually, with a conclusion.

explanation: Land reform changed who holds land; its effects depend on capital, skills, support and secure tenure.
hints: Compare the aims, size and tenure of the two models.
For (c), give benefits and problems, then a balanced conclusion.
